Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing knowledge-base entries from a fixed set of sources. It uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries, each with 2-12 cited references. Every entry is drafted from exactly the papers its curators cited, with the causal gene withheld. One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes every draft under shared guards, a shared claim-level audit and shared scoring, so only the generation strategy varies. The strategies are three paradigms (direct reading or an agentic curator; extraction into an evidence graph or a case table before writing; recall then verify), a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, a learned curation guide, a reconciled case database). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists. These lists were split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs as deposited in ClinVar (476 paragraphs, 6,652 facts). Secondary measures are HPO synopsis F1, variant recall and precision, causal-gene F1 and inheritance agreement. Main findings: (1) On the same 46 entries, hiding full text lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (+43.7 points, CI +38.3 to +49.1), and few conveyed facts come from outside the supplied text. (2) The reading strategies are within about 2 points of each other (47.2-49.1%), comparable to a measured replicate-noise half-width of 1.0 point; only the case table's -1.9 exceeds it. (3) The strategies separate in entries with more full text, which is an observational result backed by a matched ablation in which much of the case table's deficit is attributed to extraction effort. (4) The audit catches 60 of 60 planted single-fact errors and re-flags none of the same paragraphs unaltered. (5) A memory-only control declines for newer entries. The paper also reports several measurement lessons, for example that treating stopped (safety-filtered) replies asymmetrically produced a spurious 2.1-point difference.
Strengths: Careful experimental control. The sources are fixed to the curators' reference list, the model, guards, audit and scoring are shared, and the generation strategy is the only variable. This isolates the question better than most comparisons of RAG, long-context and graph pipelines, which also vary retrieval.

The within-paper access manipulation (Section 4.1, Figure 2) is the strongest result: same papers, same 2,120 fixed facts, a paired difference with a CI, repaired and unrepaired arms reported separately, and every missed and conveyed fact attributed against the available text (Figures 3, Table 16). It turns an expected direction into a measured effect size.

Unusually honest statistics for this area. The paper reports paired bootstrap CIs, better/worse/tied counts, sign tests and Holm correction, a replicate-noise floor from three full regenerations on 30 entries (Table 17: within-entry SD 5.0 giving a half-width of 1.0 over 93, which checks out arithmetically) and judge variation. It states plainly that a single run cannot rank the reading strategies.
Fixing fact lists once, before any draft is seen, avoids strategy-dependent denominators, and the paper shows that splitting afresh moves levels by 2-5 points.

Completion is treated as an outcome. The safety-filter asymmetry between one-call and per-paper strategies is identified, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis is included, and the spurious 2.1-point deficit from the earlier rule is reported. This is a useful methodological lesson for others comparing LLM pipelines.
The matched ablation (Section 4.6) separates representation from extraction effort, so the case table is not blamed for a deficit that partly comes from a lower-effort extractor.

Contamination is taken seriously: a memory-only control by creation era, a held-out set of entries created in 2026, and an explicit statement that neither shows the reading results are free of memorisation.

Limitations are thorough and specific. The paper says explicitly that the reference covers a minority of draft content (24% of statements have a counterpart) and that the audit checks fidelity, not correctness.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Drafts, audit verdicts, fact splits, fact-presence judgements and provenance attributions all come from the same model family that wrote the drafts, and no curator or annotator checked even a small sample. The headline numbers (79.8% vs 36.1%, 1.7% from outside the text, 60/60 planted errors caught) are therefore model-judged quantities. For a benchmark contribution, a modest human agreement study (for example 200-300 fact judgements and audit verdicts) is the expected minimum, and self-preference bias (Panickssery et al., cited by the authors) is a specific concern.

Single model, single run per entry. Whether the main claim (strategy matters little compared with access) holds for other model families, and especially for weaker or smaller-context models where extraction or agentic reading might help more, is untested. A finding about 'strategies' that rests on one frontier model with a context large enough for every input limits generality, and the paper says so. The regime (2-12 references, everything fits in one prompt) is also the one where direct long-context reading is expected to be hardest to beat.

The primary endpoint is narrow and indirect. It covers only variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs, which match about a quarter of draft statements. Strategies that differ mainly in how they handle phenotype narrative, cross-paper synthesis or organisation could differ on content the endpoint does not score. The secondary measures (HPO F1 against a mostly non-OMIM annotation set, gene, inheritance) only partly fill this gap.

The central access finding is largely expected. Curators wrote from full papers, so drafts from abstracts convey less of what they wrote, as the paper acknowledges. Its value lies in the effect size and the attribution, but the conclusion that 'access bounds agreement' is close to definitional for a reference written from full text. A stronger test would score against content stated in the abstract, or would use a reference not derived from full text.

The 'strategies separate where more full text is readable' result rests on 21 entries in an observational grouping confounded with era and journal. The matched ablation, the controlled check, gives a different picture for the evidence graph: on the 40 full-text-weighted entries it is +1.0 to +1.8 against direct reading, while Figure 4 shows -1.8 in the top group. The paper does not reconcile these, so the 'separation' claim in the abstract and conclusion looks stronger than the evidence.

The audit validation is weak as a test. Planted errors are single-token rule-based changes (a count, zygosity, residue or inheritance mode) in short paragraphs the audit had already passed, which is the easiest case. Omissions, misattributed citations, subtle conflation across papers and unsupported generalisations, the realistic failure modes, are untested, as acknowledged. 60/60 should not be read as audit sensitivity.

Limited relevance and novelty for ICLR. The contribution is an evaluation of prompt-level pipelines on one biomedical curation task with one proprietary model. There is no new method, and the general lessons (measure noise, fix denominators, handle failures symmetrically) are good practice but not new. The audience is closer to bioinformatics or biocuration venues, or a datasets and benchmarks track, than to the ICLR main track.

Reproducibility is limited by design: one proprietary model through a CLI with no temperature or seed control, a reference whose curated text cannot be redistributed, and safety-filter stops whose reasons are not visible. Releasing drafts and scores helps, but the benchmark cannot be re-run against new models unless the curated reference is rebuilt.

Presentation is very dense. The abstract and introduction pack many numbers, qualifiers and parentheticals into long sentences, and switching between means over entries and pooled-over-facts figures (36.1% vs 31.2%, 79.8% vs 77.3/77.4%) forces repeated re-reading. The core message would come through more clearly with fewer numbers up front and a cleaner split between primary results and caveats. Minor: the provenance counts for abstract-only papers (1,061+222+102+24 = 1,409) do not sum to the stated 1,420, and the remainder is not explained.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even on a small sample: for example agreement of a domain expert with the model's fact-presence judgements, its audit verdicts and its 'stated in available text' attributions? Without this, how should readers weigh possible self-preference in the audit and scoring?

In the matched ablation the evidence graph is ahead of direct reading (+1.0 original, +1.8 matched) on 40 full-text-weighted entries, but in Figure 4 it trails by 1.8 points in the 'half or more full text' group. How do the 21 top-group entries relate to the 40 ablation entries, and which result should readers take as the evidence-graph effect where full text is plentiful?
Have you run even a subset of the comparison with a second model family, or with a smaller-context model, to test whether the closeness of the reading strategies depends on the model?
What happens to the 11 abstract-only conveyed facts missing from the provenance breakdown (1,420 vs 1,409)?

Did you measure coverage restricted to facts that are stated in the supplied text? This would separate a strategy's reading quality from the access ceiling and would be a more sensitive test for differences between strategies.

The memory-only control names the causal gene with an F1 of about 84% overall. Does gene recall from the header alone interact with the reading strategies, for example by priming what the writer extracts? Did you look at whether entries where memory recalls the gene show smaller differences between strategies?
Limitations: The authors list limitations comprehensively: one model family, no human validation, a narrow reference, open-access text only, the regime of entries that fit one prompt, a small held-out set, and the audit untested on omissions.
Not fully discussed: the planted-error test covers only the easiest error type, and the observational full-text separation conflicts with the ablation for the evidence graph.
Thought: This is a carefully controlled and unusually honest evaluation. It has paired CIs and a measured replicate noise floor (SD 5.0 giving 1.0 over 93, which checks out), handles completion symmetrically and admits its limits. But every judgement comes from the writer's own model family with zero human validation, and only one model is tested. The primary reference covers about a quarter of draft content. The main positive finding (abstracts convey less of what curators wrote from full text) is close to expected, and the 'strategies separate with more full text' claim rests on 21 observational entries that conflict with the ablation for the evidence graph (+1.0/+1.8 there vs -1.8 in Fig 4). ML novelty for the ICLR main track is limited; this is a domain benchmark of prompt pipelines. The writing is extremely dense. I lean reject but could be persuaded by human validation and a second model.
